newsitem.title: JORDAN: Netanyahu presses Arafat for security action.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu presses Arafat for security action.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday he was ready to ease sanctions against Palestinians once President Yasser Arafat begins cracking down on Moslem militants.

"What we would like to see is the fulfilment of the commitment to battle the terrorists and as we see action, any action taken in that direction, we shall adjust and change our measures accordingly," Netanyahu told a joint news conference with Jordan's King Hussein.
Netanyahu met King Hussein in the Red Sea resort of Aqaba on the crisis in Israeli-Palestinian ties since a double suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market last month.
Israel sealed off the Gaza Strip and West Bank after the July 30 bombing, which killed 14 people and the two bombers.
Palestinians say the closure causes them extreme economic hardship and makes them prisoners in the territories.
"The measures which we have been forced to take as a result of the recent tragedy in Jerusalem are meant to assure security and not to act in any way against the Palestinian people," Netanyahu said.
He said he had information that militants were planning more attacks in Israel.
The Jewish state blames Moslem militants for the attack and has accused Arafat of failing to crack down on militants operating from self-rule areas.
Arafat has insisted he is making a "100 percent effort" on security and accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to weaken his legitimacy.
King Hussein said the Middle East was passing through "a very dangerous moment."

"I am convinced as I have always thought in the past that (Netanyahu) is a partner for peace and he is committed to it and hopefully he will be able, together with his colleagues to make their full contribution to peace, through the cessation of one and all of acts that jeopardise peace," the king said.
Netanyahu, in his first meeting with an Arab leader since the attack, also said he was willing to discuss the fate of Jewish settlements in occupied areas in peace talks with the Palestinians.

"We can and we will discuss our differences, including on the issues of settlements, around the negotiating table...and hopefully come to a final settlement and end once and for all the conflict between Israelis and Palestinians," Netanyahu said.
He appeared to adopt more conciliatory language on peace talks, including references to the Palestinians as "partners".
Peace talks between the parties had been deadlocked since March when Israel broke ground on a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The fate of Jewish settlements on land occupied by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war is one of the most contentious issues in any final peace deal.
U.S. mediator Dennis Ross has shuttled between Netanyahu and Arafat since Sunday, managing to bring Israeli and Palestinian security officials together for intelligence sharing.
But the Palestinian side links security cooperation with political progress in peacemaking and demands a halt to Israeli settlement building in the West Bank.
Ross said he believed Israel would ease its closure once security cooperation resumed.

"I think that as security cooperation goes forward I believe that in fact you'll see an easing of the measures," he told CNN in an interview in Jerusalem before the Netanyahu-King Hussein news conference.

Ross was expected to meet again with Arafat and Netanyahu on Wednesday before heading home to prepare a possible first visit to the region by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright later this month.
